input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

output:
We evaluate section outputs along three complementary axes designed to quantify citation fidelity and factual consistency while remaining auditable and reproducible: (1) citation coverage, (2) hallucination rate (unsupported assertions), and (3) reviewer-style quality scores. The measurements and procedures described below are the operational definitions and annotation protocol used in this study; they are author-defined for the present experiments.

Metric definitions

- Citation coverage. For a given generated section, citation coverage is operationalized as the proportion of content units that the annotator or automated routine deems to require explicit evidence and that are accompanied by at least one documented source in the section’s machine-readable output (the section JSON “evidence” field or inline citation key in the assembled LaTeX). Content units can be sentences or finer-grained assertions depending on the annotation granularity chosen prior to evaluation. This metric is intended to reflect whether claims that should be grounded carry explicit, traceable citations.

- Hallucination rate (unsupported assertions). The hallucination rate is the proportion of judged content units that lack adequate support in the available evidence pool. An assertion is labeled “unsupported” when none of the provided sources (those injected at generation time and any external index returned by retrieval) contain a passage that directly substantiates the factual claim according to the annotation guidelines described below. This metric focuses on unsupported factual claims rather than stylistic or editorial issues.

- Reviewer-style quality scores. We collect ordinal reviewer judgments on several dimensions that are complementary to the automated metrics: factuality (degree to which claims are accurate and supported), citation adequacy (appropriateness and sufficiency of cited sources), coherence (local logical flow within the section and consistency with parent/child sections in the document graph), and overall acceptability for inclusion in a draft manuscript. Reviewers assign ordinal labels according to a fixed rubric; these labels are used for qualitative calibration and for aggregated summary statistics.

Annotation and audit procedure

- Annotation unit and guidelines. Prior to annotation we define the atomic unit of evaluation (sentence or atomic assertion). Annotators receive the generated section, the section JSON (including any evidence list), and the assembled LaTeX with the refs.bib file. Annotators mark each unit as (a) supported: at least one cited source contains text that directly substantiates the claim, (b) partially supported: cited sources are only indirectly related or require inference, or (c) unsupported: no cited or retrievable source substantiates the claim. The guideline emphasizes conservative judgments: indirect or speculative links are treated as partial support at best.

- Adjudication and reliability. Each item is annotated by multiple independent annotators. Disagreements on binary supported/unsupported labels are resolved through adjudication by a third reviewer who consults the available evidence pool and the JSON provenance fields. We record inter-annotator disagreement and adjudication outcomes to characterize annotation reliability; these records also form an auditable trail.

- Audit logs and provenance. All annotations, adjudication notes, and the mapping from content units to evidence items are stored alongside the machine-readable section JSON as an audit log. This enables post-hoc inspection of why a unit was judged unsupported and which evidence items were considered.

Automated measurement and integration with machine-readable outputs

- Automation via JSON and LaTeX/bib. The system’s strict JSON schema for sections and the deterministic LaTeX+refs.bib assembly enable automated computation of several metrics. For citation coverage, an automated routine parses the section JSON to enumerate declared assertions or sentences, checks for non-empty evidence lists on each item, and computes the proportion covered. For hallucination detection, automated heuristics flag units with empty evidence lists or with evidence whose provenance metadata indicates low retrieval relevance; flagged units are then prioritized for manual annotation. The assembled refs.bib provides a deterministic mapping from inline citation keys to bibliographic entries, which simplifies automated checks for missing bib entries or unresolved citation keys.

- Reproducibility and machine-aided auditing. Because every section output includes explicit evidence pointers and structured fields, metric computations are reproducible: the same JSON inputs and the same measurement script yield identical metric values. Audit artifacts (annotator labels, adjudication notes, and the matching evidence snippets) are exported in machine-readable form to support downstream error analysis and targeted repair.

Scoring rubric and reporting

- Ordinal scales and aggregated summaries. Reviewer-style judgments use fixed ordinal scales (predefined by the study protocol). Aggregated results are reported as distributions over scale points and accompanied by the underlying annotation counts and audit logs to avoid over-interpretation of point estimates.

- Complementary quantitative and qualitative reporting. Quantitative metrics (coverage and hallucination rates) are presented alongside representative qualitative examples chosen from the audit logs: (i) a correctly supported claim with its cited evidence, (ii) a partially supported claim illustrating acceptable indirect linkage, and (iii) an unsupported hallucination with annotator rationale. Examples are accompanied by the annotated JSON fragment and bibliographic provenance to permit verifiable inspection.

Limitations and conservative interpretation

- Scope of claims. The evaluation protocol is intentionally conservative: support requires explicit, traceable evidence and annotators favor labeling borderline cases as unsupported. This design reduces false positives in coverage estimates but can increase measured hallucination rates relative to looser criteria.

- Dataset and annotation constraints. The present evaluation is driven by the available curated materials and the annotation budget; results reported in the paper should be interpreted in this context. All annotation decisions, adjudication logs, and metric computation scripts are retained to facilitate transparent re-analysis.

Note on grounding. The operational definitions and procedures above are the study’s author-defined evaluation protocol. No external retrieval artifacts or third‑party excerpts were required to specify this protocol; all measurement procedures and schema-driven automation are internal to the experiment design.
